title: Joshua 2:8–14
context: Before the spies lie down, Rahab comes to them on the roof and confesses that she knows the LORD has given Israel the land. She reports the terror that has fallen on the inhabitants after they heard how the LORD dried up the Red Sea and how Israel utterly destroyed Sihon and Og beyond the Jordan, and she confesses that the LORD, Israel’s God, is God in heaven above and on earth beneath. On that basis she asks the men to swear by the LORD to deal kindly with her father’s house, to give her a true sign, and to save her family from death. They pledge their life for hers, on condition that she not talk about their business, and they promise to deal kindly and truly with her when the LORD gives them the land. Both traditions, with Hebrews 11:31 and James 2:25, read Rahab’s confession as genuine faith and her request as faith seeking mercy for her household. The land promise is acknowledged even here as the LORD’s gift. The destruction named in verse 10 is the already-past defeat of the two Amorite kings, not the coming herem of Canaanite cities.

verses.text: Before they had lain down, she came up to them on the roof.
verses.arminianNotes:
Before the spies have lain down, Rahab comes up to them on the roof. The hiding place becomes a place of speech; she seeks them out before they sleep.

Arminian readers hear her initiative. She is not only concealing them; she is coming to confess and to ask, and the next verses will give her words at length.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise mark the pause “Before they had lain down,” when she comes up to them. The decisive conversation is hers to begin, and it will reveal what she has already come to know about the LORD.

Both traditions take the verse as the turn from concealment to confession, shared narrative ground.

verses.text: She said to the men, “I know that the LORD has given you the land, and that the fear of you has fallen upon us, and that all the inhabitants of the land melt away before you.
verses.arminianNotes:
She says, “I know that the LORD has given you the land, and that the fear of you has fallen upon us, and that all the inhabitants of the land melt away before you.”

Arminian readers hear a real confession of knowledge. She uses the LORD’s name and speaks of the gift as already given; fear is present, but so is a clear acknowledgment of what God has done.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress “I know” and the already-given land. The terror on the inhabitants is the fruit of the LORD’s prior works, and her knowledge is a hearing-faith that those works have produced.

Both traditions, with Hebrews 11:31, take this as the beginning of genuine faith, not as mere bargaining talk, though her fear is real and unhidden.

verses.text: For we have heard how the LORD dried up the water of the Red Sea before you, when you came out of Egypt; and what you did to the two kings of the Amorites, who were beyond the Jordan, to Sihon and to Og, whom you utterly destroyed.
verses.arminianNotes:
The ground of her knowledge is what “we have heard”: the LORD dried up the water of the Red Sea when Israel came out of Egypt, and Israel utterly destroyed Sihon and Og, the two Amorite kings beyond the Jordan.

Arminian readers hear faith coming by the report of God’s mighty works. She names the exodus and the already-finished defeat of those two kings; the herem in Canaan has not yet begun.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise trace her confession to the hearing of the LORD’s acts. “utterly destroyed” here looks back to Sihon and Og, not forward to Jericho; the verse is testimony, not a new command of destruction.

Both traditions keep that past reference clear and take the hearing of God’s works as the means by which her knowledge has come.

verses.text: As soon as we had heard it, our hearts melted, and there wasn’t any more spirit in any man, because of you: for the LORD your God, he is God in heaven above, and on earth beneath.
verses.arminianNotes:
“As soon as we had heard it, our hearts melted, and there wasn’t any more spirit in any man, because of you: for the LORD your God, he is God in heaven above, and on earth beneath.”

Arminian readers hear a high, personal confession. She does not stop at fear; she confesses that Israel’s God is God in heaven and on earth, a genuine turning toward him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same words as a confession of the LORD’s unique deity, close to the language of the law. Hearts melt at the hearing, and from that hearing comes the acknowledgment that he is God above and below.

Both traditions take the confession as true faith in the one God, which Hebrews 11:31 will later praise, shared ground not to be reduced to panic alone.

verses.text: Now therefore, please swear to me by the LORD, since I have dealt kindly with you, that you also will deal kindly with my father’s house, and give me a true sign;
verses.arminianNotes:
She asks them to swear by the LORD, since she has dealt kindly with them, that they will also deal kindly with her father’s house and give her a true sign.

Arminian readers hear faith seeking mercy, and not only for herself. She binds the request to the LORD’s name and to the kindness she has already shown; she wants a real pledge and a visible sign.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the oath in the LORD’s name and the language of kindness, the mercy of a sworn bond. She asks to be brought under Israel’s pledged care, and she asks for “a true sign” that will mark that pledge.

Both traditions take the request as faith reaching toward a covenant promise for her household, not as a mere commercial bargain.

verses.text: and that you will save alive my father, my mother, my brothers, and my sisters, and all that they have, and will deliver our lives from death.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The kindness she seeks is specific: that they will save alive her father, mother, brothers, and sisters, and all that they have, and will deliver their lives from death.

Arminian readers hear intercession for a whole household. Her faith is not a private escape plan; she pleads for her family’s life, and the spies will have to answer that plea.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise note the width of the request: parents, siblings, possessions, and lives. The deliverance she asks is from death in the coming judgment on the city, and it is asked under the oath of verse 12.

Both traditions take the household plea as part of her faith, without turning the family itself into a forced symbol of the church.

verses.text: The men said to her, “Our life for yours, if you don’t talk about this business of ours; and it shall be, when the LORD gives us the land, that we will deal kindly and truly with you.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The men say, “Our life for yours, if you don’t talk about this business of ours; and it shall be, when the LORD gives us the land, that we will deal kindly and truly with you.”

Arminian readers hear a real, conditional oath. They stake their lives, they require her silence, and they promise kindness and truth when God gives the land—a promise they must later keep.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress “when the LORD gives us the land,” as the setting of their pledge. The spies share Rahab’s confession that the gift is the LORD’s, and they bind themselves to kindness and truth under that certainty.

Both traditions take the pledge as a true oath in the LORD’s purpose, with a real condition attached, shared ground for the sign that follows.
